Monumental interior of a contemporary semiconductor fabrication facility, a massive EUV lithography scanner at the luminous center, architecture fractured into vast overlapping prisms and crystalline planes, cubist industrial modernism fused with Soviet monumental painting. Radiant golden white plasma light erupts through the machine like a technological sun, angular beams cutting across lavender haze, steel blue shadows and pearlescent cleanroom whites. Colossal ventilation ducts, vacuum chambers, utility pipes, gantries, and overhead FOUP transport rails form a dense geometric symphony. Tiny cleanroom technicians in white bunny suits silhouetted on elevated walkways convey immense scale. Sterile precision rendered with vigorous painterly brushwork, translucent layers, smoky edges, faceted reflections. Simultaneously utopian and overwhelming, the fab portrayed as the blast furnace of the information age. Abstract yet architecturally convincing, museum scale oil painting. No text, no logos, no readable signage. --chaos 22 --ar 4:5 --stylize 650 --weird 180 --v 8.2

OpenAl confirmed to the New York Times that they have made "substantial progress" on another Millennium Prize problem in the last five days, and are preparing to announce.
The rumors for the last 48 hours have been OpenAl solved the Hodge Conjecture, and that Anthropic has solved the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture. Since Navier-Stokes rumors abound, so I was reluctant to post about either.
However, OpenAl's statement to the NYT now gives the Hodge rumors some very serious support.
In general people have not updated yet that the new unnamed OpenAl model, the one that finished training about two weeks ago, which I believe will be named Aeon, is massively better at math than Astra, which two weeks ago was the best in the world. Aeon solved Navier-Stokes in 88 hours, start to finish. Follow the trend line.
That means everything is on the table. Literally everything. And this does not end with math.
Please update. We are taking off.

A line and scatter plot titled "FrontierCode 1.1 Main: Score vs Cost ($)" comparing AI model performance against expense.
Axes
 * Y-axis: Score (%), ranging from 35 to 55.
 * X-axis: Average cost (USD) per rollout, ranging from $0.00 to $10.00 in increments of $2.00.
Model Performance Data
 * SWE-2 (blue curve): Shows high efficiency, rising steeply from approximately 43% score at $0.20 to 50% score at $1.20.
 * GPT-6 Astra (green line): Reaches the highest peak performance at approximately 53.5% score for a cost around $4.30.
 * Fable 5.1 (orange line): Ranges between 49% and 51% score across costs from $2.50 to $9.30.
 * GPT-5.6 Sol (teal line): Climbs from 35.5% score at $2.10 to 47.5% score at $6.30.
 * Grok 4.6 (grey line): Scales from 40% score at $1.00 to 48% score at $3.10.
 * Kimi K3 (purple point): Placed around 44% score at $3.80.
 * SWE-1.7 (blue point): Placed around 42% score at $2.00.
Footnotes
 * Score: A weighted aggregate of the rubric items. Solutions that don't pass blocking criteria receive 0.
 * Cost ($): The mean USD spend per rollout.
